item.title: Transformer-Based Characterization of Criticality in Directed Percolation
item.description: arXiv:2611.08527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Directed percolation (DP) provides a canonical framework for studying nonequilibrium phase transitions into absorbing states, yet extracting critical behavior directly from high-dimensional spatiotemporal configurations remains challenging. Here, we investigate (1 + 1)- and (2 + 1)-dimensional bond DP using a supervised Transformer encoder. Supervised learning results demonstrate that the Transformer can distinguish between the active and absorbing phases of directed percolation with high accuracy. The critical point and critical exponents estimated from the model's classification probabilities align closely with reference values from existing literature, indicating that the model not only achieves phase classification but also yields outputs containing information related to critical scaling behavior. To probe the model's internal representation, we employ attention rollout and define an attention center that quantifies the temporal centroid of the cumulative attention distribution. The attention patterns and the attention center reorganize systematically near the critical region and exhibit pronounced finite-size dependence. Finally, we examined the model's transferability between configurations generated from fully occupied initial states and those from single-seed initial states. The results indicate the presence of transferable information between the two types of data, though the transfer performance exhibits directional asymmetry. Furthermore, when using an equal amount of target-domain data, fine-tuning yielded only a marginal improvement in accuracy compared to training from scratch.
item.dc:creator: Bozheng Dou, Wei Li

item.title: Nonequilibrium Fluctuations and Intrinsic Stability of Nanostructured Solar Cells: Microscopic Derivation and Universal Laws
item.description: arXiv:2611.08529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study nonequilibrium fluctuations of efficiency in nanostructured solar cells. Our contribution is threefold. First, we derive a microscopic stochastic model of efficiency from a two-state master equation describing absorption, radiative recombination, and extraction. This derivation establishes an explicit link between efficiency fluctuations and entropy production, and justifies the thermodynamic affinity through local detailed balance. Second, we review universal fluctuation laws established in the recent literature and apply them for the first time to the real parameters of nanostructured solar cells. We show that the total entropy production behaves as a submartingale, and that its negative exponential is a martingale. For a biased discrete random walk, the exact infimum law is verified numerically in the near-equilibrium regime, then applied to realistic solar cell configurations. Third, our simulations show that nanostructured solar cells operate in a strongly nonequilibrium regime, where negative entropy fluctuations, and hence efficiency fluctuations, are exponentially rare. Over all simulated trajectories, most configurations show no detectable negative fluctuation, consistent with the theoretical prediction. These results explain the intrinsic statistical stability of the devices and provide a conceptual and quantitative framework for understanding efficiency fluctuations around the mean values. They do not modify the mean efficiencies obtained previously, but clarify their statistical robustness in the strongly nonequilibrium regime.
item.dc:creator: Rivo Herivola Manjakamanana Ravelonjato, Ravo Tokiniaina Ranaivoson, Philipe Manjakasoa Randriantsoa, Raoelina Andriambololona, Wilfrid Chrysante Solofoarisina

item.title: Permutation order governs basin entropy in critical one-input Boolean networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.08532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Basin entropy measures uncertainty about a network's long-term behavior. For every critical one-input synchronous Boolean network with $m$ relevant nodes, we show that the permutation structure induced by its feedback loops determines basin entropy, up to a universal error. Although the loops oscillate independently, their relative phases can be offset, producing a deviation from additivity that can grow linearly in $m$. Yet at the ensemble level, a previously derived additive prediction is preserved through the first subleading term, with the discrepancy appearing at order $\ln m\ln\ln m$.
item.dc:creator: Ruodan Liu, Ahana Ghosh, Sean Campbell, Venkata Sai Narayana Bavisetty, Matthew Wheeler, Claus Kadelka

item.title: Interacting particles crossing barriers: spatial statistics, choice of route taken and role of interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.08617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the statistics of pairs of particles moving in a potential energy landscape exhibiting a choice of different pathways from a local minimum start point to the global energy minimum destination. We examine the impact of both attractive and repulsive interactions between the particles, treating these via either a soft Gaussian or a Lennard-Jones potential. We investigate the statistics of which particle arrives at the destination first, arrival-time distributions and where in the system the second particle is located when the first arrives. We find that the typical arrival time of the first particle can be significantly different to that of a single particle, sometimes being much longer and in other cases being shorter, depending on the nature of the particle interactions. In the case of soft Gaussian attractive interactions, which effectively bind the pair of particles together to form a single larger particle, the arrival time can be much longer, since bigger particles cross barriers more slowly. In contrast, the arrival time is shorter when there is a repulsive core interaction between the particles, due to excluded-area and particle-ordering effects. We investigate the probability distribution of particles' positions through the Jensen--Shannon divergence which unveils the dependence of the spatial distribution of the particles within the confining potential on the parameters of the particle interaction potentials.
item.dc:creator: Gulzar Ahmad, Andrew J Archer, Sergey Savel'ev, Marco G Mazza

item.title: $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge and exact solution of the $\pm J$ Edwards-Anderson model in a transverse field
item.description: arXiv:2611.09097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using the Majorana representation of spin-1/2 operators, we study the $\pm J$ Edwards--Anderson model in a transverse field at $T=0$. We show that, in this representation, the quantity describing the coupling between neighboring spins commutes with the Hamiltonian and, unlike in the Kitaev model, is not subject to any Gauss law. The resulting $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge freedom allows the disorder in the signs of the exchange integrals to be eliminated by an exact gauge transformation, so that the spectrum of the system coincides with that of the model with uniform couplings. The resulting theory is quadratic in the Majorana fields. Computing the local Green's functions, we find that the Edwards--Anderson order parameter vanishes for $\Delta>J\sqrt{Z}$ and equals $1/4$ for $\Delta<J\sqrt{Z}$, which signals a second-order transition from a paramagnetic phase to a spin-glass ground state that is degenerate over spin configurations and replica symmetric at $T=0$.
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Vasin

item.title: Thermalization of coarse-grained variables in the Toda lattice: a numerical study
item.description: arXiv:2611.09287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present here a numerical study of the Toda lattice Hamiltonian dynamics showing how, despite model integrability, it is possible to find many macroscopic observables which display standard equilibrium behavior. In particular, we study numerically the energy time correlation of certain coarse-grained variables, showing that it decays with either exponential or stretched exponential behaviour, thus indicating good thermalization properties. The spirit of our observation is complementary to that of standard Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou-like numerical experiments, in which the breaking of integrability is regarded as the key ingredient for relaxation to thermal equilibrium. The present communication corroborates, on the contrary, the view that integrability is not an obstacle to thermalization, provided that a sufficiently weak definition of the latter is accepted. In the Toda lattice we have introduced several kinds of coarse-grained variables, constructed with the purpose to maintain a thermodynamic relevance also for large system sizes, which all show good thermalization properties.
item.dc:creator: Martina Giachello, Cesare Vianello, Giacomo Gradenigo

item.title: Mathematical analysis of the Markovian Mpemba effect
item.description: arXiv:2611.09391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mpemba effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon in which two equilibrium systems at different temperatures, say hot and warm systems, when quenched at the same bath temperature, for some pair of hot and warm temperatures, the hot system comes to bath temperature faster than the warm system. In recent years, studies on the Mpemba effect for Markovian systems under external potential, which are continuous-time, continuous-state-space Markov processes, have been carried out theoretically and experimentally by resorting to pseudo-distance measures which are not true distance metrics. Moreover, maximum crossover time is given for the Mpemba effect for all monotone distance measures or functions (which include true distance metrics and pseudo-distance measures). However, no mathematical analysis is carried out for the mere possibility of the presence of the Mpemba effect for Markovian systems under an external potential with a true distance metric. In this paper, by using a true distance metric which arises naturally from the weighted Hilbert space in which the adjoint of the generator of the Markov process is a Hermitian operator, we have shown the mathematical analysis of the possibility of the presence of the Mpemba effect by using Poincar\'e inequality and the geometry of Hilbert space.
item.dc:creator: Umashankar Pardhi, Syed Abbas, Moupriya Das

item.title: Thermodynamics of Speed and Efficiency with Quantum Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.08564v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rapid thermodynamic operations generally entail irreversible dissipation, giving rise to trade-offs between operating speed and thermodynamic cost. Yet, how quantum feedback fundamentally reshapes these trade-offs remains elusive. Here, we derive a finite-time current--dissipation relation for continuously monitored open quantum dynamics with jump feedback. From this fundamental relation, we establish a quantum speed limit and a power-efficiency trade-off for stationary information engines, identifying how feedback affects state transformations and the performance of engines through both informational entropy and direct dynamical contributions. Our results provide a quantitative foundation for fast, low-dissipation quantum thermodynamics in the presence of feedback control, exemplified by attaining the generalized Landauer bound in finite-time information erasure and approaching unit information efficiency at finite power in the large-system limit of a collective engine.
item.dc:creator: Yue Liu, Ryotaro Honma, Ruicheng Bao, Tan Van Vu

item.title: Analytic Bounds on Conformal Defect Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2611.08582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conformal defects describe impurities and boundaries at criticality. Their stability depends on the scaling dimensions of operators localized on the defects, but these dimensions are often difficult to determine. We derive analytic upper bounds on the lowest nonvacuum scaling dimension using only two defect entropies and the dimension of a defect-changing operator. The bounds identify when relevant operators must appear on the defect with larger defect entropy. They follow from the conformal bootstrap of four-point functions of defect-changing operators and apply to unitary conformal line defects and to conformal boundaries in two-dimensional CFTs. The Ising and Potts models provide exact checks. In three-dimensional $O(N)$ models, we apply the bounds to direct sums of pinning field defects with symmetry-related orientations. Data from a single such defect exclude stable impurity order with three or more orientations in $O(2)$ and $O(3)$, or four or more in $O(4)$, for any geometry of the orientations, and require a relevant domain-wall operator between individually stable pinning field defects at every nonzero relative angle up to $120^\circ$ in $O(3)$ and up to $109.47^\circ$ in $O(4)$. A direct fuzzy-sphere computation of the lowest domain-wall dimension at different relative angles for $N=2,3,4$ is consistent with these bounds and indicates that, within this class of impurities, only two-state order remains a candidate for stable order in $O(3)$ and $O(4)$, while none survives in $O(2)$. A separate application to AdS/BCFT shows that, at fixed unequal brane tensions, a light boundary-condition-changing operator requires additional light primaries on the boundary with larger boundary entropy.
item.dc:creator: Yuma Furuta, Wataru Harada, Yuya Kusuki, Yin Tang

item.title: Fortuitous Cancellation of Competing Effects in the Free Energy of Water Autoionization: Long-Range Electrostatics, System Size, and Nuclear Quantum Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.08874v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Few molecular processes are more fundamental to chemistry than the autoionization of water, whose equilibrium constant, $K_w \approx 10^{-14}$, underlies acid-base equilibria and the chemistry of life. Yet the molecular origins of the free energy cost of forming and separating ions remain incompletely understood. Efforts to explain it have been limited by the difficulty of modeling water reactivity in sufficient detail. Here we combine machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with spectral adaptive biasing force enhanced sampling to connect proton transfer and water wire configurations to the underlying free energy landscape. We identify competing influences of long-range electrostatics, system size, temperature, and nuclear quantum motion on the predicted ionization thermodynamics. The free energy surface extends from neutral water to ions separated beyond the solvent-separated ion pair (SSIP). It reveals a transition state in which a proton is shared between the second and third molecules of a three-membered water wire. The contact ion pair is unstable and the SSIP only weakly metastable, so determining pK$_w$ requires sampling longer wires. Long-range electrostatics raise the free energy at ion separations beyond $3\,\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$. Models with comparable force errors give substantially different free energy profiles in this region. Increasing system size lowers the calculated pK$_w$, while nuclear quantum effects bring it closer to experiment and reproduce the higher pK$_w$ of D$_2$O relative to H$_2$O. These results establish a baseline for interpreting thermodynamic results from MLIP simulations in which charged and polar groups react and diffuse in finite cells. Our analysis also explains how cancellation among competing effects can yield ionization constants close to experiment even when simulations omit several physical contributions.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Varner, Yinan Xu, Yezhi Jin, Gustavo R. P\'erez-Lemus, Pablo F. Zubieta Rico, Zhiying Yi, Joan M. Montes de Oca, Paul F. Nealey, Seth B. Darling, Zhen-Gang Wang, Juan J. de Pablo

item.title: Optimal asymptotic pure-state conversion under thermal operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.08974v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum thermodynamics seeks to characterize possible state transformations under thermodynamic constraints in microscopic quantum systems. In the fully quantum regime, however, quantum coherence imposes various restrictions on state conversions, and a complete characterization of state convertibility has remained open. Here we resolve this problem for asymptotic conversions between pure states. Specifically, we show that asymptotic convertibility is fully determined by the free-energy and energy-variance ratios. Our result reveals how genuinely quantum effects quantitatively constrain state conversions in quantum thermodynamics.
item.dc:creator: Tatsuya Yamanouchi, Naoto Shiraishi

item.title: Perfect Wave Transfer in Nonconformal Tomonaga-Luttinger Liquids
item.description: arXiv:2611.09018v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Perfect wave transfer (PWT) reproduces spatial reflection at a common finite time under a fixed Hamiltonian. We classify this process for open compact bosons and inhomogeneous Tomonaga--Luttinger liquids, distinguishing transfer of oscillator and neutral observables from transfer on the charged field algebra. In the single-charge model, the first two notions coincide. Global transfer additionally requires rephasing of the compact zero mode. For regular reflection-symmetric channels, exact oscillator transfer forces an odd multiple of the optical crossing time and a strictly ordered, parity-compatible spectrum differing from the conformal ladder at only finitely many levels. This spectral condition is also sufficient when the Robin boundary data induced by the physical profile are included. Requiring Neumann conditions after the Liouville transformation instead forces conformality. We construct an explicit, regular one-defect family for every $r>1/2$. Its transfer parameters are precisely the reduced fractions $r=p/q$ with odd numerator and denominator, with shortest transfer time $pL/v_0$. At the delay $3L/v_0$, the $r=3/5$ profile has numerical contrast $K_{\max}/K_{\min}\simeq 12.913$, compared with $81$ for $r=3$. Two independent conservative discretizations show second-order convergence on fixed mode bands. Occupation- and charge-constrained error estimates quantify robustness, while an exact homogeneous-chain calculation explains the $J^{2/3}$ resolved-band scale also observed in the engineered channels. These results provide a spectral design method and finite-device benchmarks for quadratic quantum channels. An interacting microscopic realization remains open.
item.dc:creator: Davide Batic, Denys Dutykh

item.title: Deep Learning Theory through the Lens of Statistical Physics: A Topical Review
item.description: arXiv:2611.09138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The recent success of foundation models and deep learning has far outpaced our theoretical understanding of how large-scale neural networks learn and generalize. Statistical physics provides a natural language for describing such high-dimensional, nonlinear, and strongly coupled systems, offering concepts such as mean-field theory, phase transitions, energy landscapes, and stochastic dynamics. In this topical review, we adopt a statistical-physics way of thinking -- from concepts including phases and criticality, and free-energy viewpoints, to methods such as kernel and Gaussian-process limits, mean-field and dynamical mean-field theories, random-matrix tools, and Fokker-Planck formalisms, and to a mindset emphasizing universality, scaling, and tractable limits with explicit validity regimes. We survey recent progress on understanding modern deep learning through this lens, including mean-field analyses of wide networks, spectral and geometric perspectives on loss landscapes, stochastic-gradient-based training viewed as a dynamical process, and phase-transition analogies that organize phenomena such as overparameterization, generalization, and representation change. Our goal is to synthesize these threads into a coherent framework that clarifies what each approximation explains, when it is expected to hold, and how apparently competing narratives relate or diverge. Together, these perspectives form a unified physical framework that views representation learning as a collective phenomenon in high-dimensional systems, bridging deterministic and stochastic regimes of gradient-based optimization.
item.dc:creator: Wei Huang, Youjin Deng

item.title: Continuum mean-field theory of spatiotemporal pattern formation in a three-state active Potts model
item.description: arXiv:2611.09180v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of a three-state active Potts model with a cyclic transition bias. Starting from microscopic Glauber-type dynamics, we derive macroscopic continuum field equations through a spatial mean-field approximation. Linear stability and weakly nonlinear analyses reveal that increasing the coupling strength induces a Hopf bifurcation, near which the critical amplitude dynamics is described by the complex Ginzburg--Landau equation. In the spatially homogeneous limit, the system exhibits limit-cycle oscillations and ordered states, with an intermediate regime of bistability bounded by a $\mathbb{Z}_3$-symmetric heteroclinic bifurcation. In two dimensions, the system sustains stable rotating spiral waves. Using perturbation theory based on one-dimensional traveling fronts, we semianalytically predict the curvature-dependent propagation velocity of circular fronts, as well as the rotational angular velocity and pitch of spiral waves. Finally, we compare the continuum model with discrete Monte Carlo simulations to clarify the role of thermal fluctuations and evaluate the validity of the mean-field approximation.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Tateyama, Songhao Yin, Hiroaki Ito, Hiroyuki Kitahata, Hiroshi Noguchi

item.title: Dynamics and pseudospectra around quantum exceptional points
item.description: arXiv:2611.09464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) are a hallmark of non-Hermitian physics, giving rise to extreme sensitivity and enhanced dynamic response. Such unique spectral singularities have been extensively studied in classical photonics, both at theoretical and experimental levels, where the relevant observables are evident. That is not necessarily the case in the quantum regime, where this kind of behavior around EPs, to a large extent, remains elusive. In fact, the interplay between dissipation and quantum fluctuations makes the complete Lindbladian evolution quite different from effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian descriptions. In this context, we investigate the signatures of the Liouvillian EPs on spectral and dynamic response by considering properly normalized long-time averages and imbalances. Even though our approach is generic, we focus on two paradigmatic models-a lossy Bose-Hubbard lattice and a dissipative two-spin system, where we investigate the role of quantum jumps and interactions in the Liouvillian spectrum, in terms of complex and structured pseudospectra. Our results demonstrate how non-Hermitian phenomena emerge in realistic quantum lattices, providing a bridge between classical EP physics and experimentally accessible open quantum systems.
item.dc:creator: Georgios E. Pavlou, Ioannis Kiorpelidis, Georgios K. Simopoulos, Manas Kulkarni, Konstantinos G. Makris

item.title: Resolving non-neutrality across scales in a hyperdiverse tropical forest
item.description: arXiv:2611.09479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Different ecological processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Macroscopic regularities can therefore be captured by descriptions that ignore microscopic details, even when those details are mechanistically relevant to ecological processes. Here, we develop a framework inspired by statistical mechanics to track interspecific spatial correlations under spatial coarse-graining. To do so we combine random-matrix filtering with a spatially explicit neutral model. Applying this approach to eight censuses of the Barro Colorado Island tropical forest, we observe a continuous crossover from an interacting to an effectively neutral organization. Below a few tens of metres (20--35~m), the empirical correlation spectrum differs from neutral expectations, revealing scale-dependent species-specific structure. Part of this structure can be attributed to environmental heterogeneity. However, residual spatial associations provide candidate signatures of biotic interactions or other unmeasured ecological, non-neutral processes. With increasing spatial coarse-graining, empirical and neutral correlation spectra progressively converge, and above the crossover scale the neutral model provides an accurate description of the measured collective organization. Neutrality thus emerges as an effective description of the collective organization of the forest above a characteristic scale, without implying that species are equivalent at the individual level. Our framework provides an operational way to locate that scale.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Zgaga, Pablo Villegas, Tancredi Caruso, Tommaso Gili

item.title: Violent relaxation redux
item.description: arXiv:2611.09531v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collisionless self-gravitating systems, such as merging galaxies, have long seemed an exception to the statistical-mechanical principle that chaotic many-body systems relax to maximum-entropy states: Lynden-Bell's statistical mechanics of their "violent relaxation," constrained by exact conservation of phase-space volume -- equivalently, of infinitely many collisionless "Casimir" invariants -- has appeared not to be a good description. We propose that violent relaxation does give rise to Lynden-Bell's maximum-entropy equilibria, but that both are underpinned by gravitational turbulence, in which large-scale gravitational fluctuations drive chaotic phase-space mixing of the particles' distribution function. We derive the universal small-scale (sub-Jeans) spectra of this turbulence and show that it leads to phase-space-volume conservation being broken on a timescale only logarithmically longer, in the particle number N, than the dynamical (violent-relaxation) time. This timescale separation lets the system relax "adiabatically" through a sequence of Lynden-Bell equilibria, each corresponding to instantaneous values of the Casimirs. At long times, it approaches an equilibrium close to its "ground state": a distribution whose Casimirs have adjusted so that the system's energy is now its minimum possible energy. Thus, the system's universal tendency is toward a minimum-energy, maximum-entropy state. We corroborate this picture with 1D N-body simulations and hypothesize that it can explain the universal equilibria of galaxies and dark-matter halos.
item.dc:creator: Michael L. Nastac, Yonadav Barry Ginat, Robert J. Ewart, Michael Barnes, Alexander A. Schekochihin

item.title: Suppression of gel formation by spontaneous fragmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work we study the discrete Smoluchowski equation with a multiplicative kernel and an additional term describing the spontaneous shattering of each particle into monomers at a constant rate $\lambda$. We show that the introduction of fragmentation suppresses gelation for $\lambda \ge 4$. We derive analytical expressions for the second moment and the monomer concentration $n_1(t)$. These expressions lead to a recurrence relation allowing the steady-state particle size distribution for $\lambda \ge 4$ to be calculated with machine precision. We validate our analytical and semi-analytical results via numerical simulations using a solver that employs the Fast Fourier Transform for computation of the right-hand side and a second-order Runge-Kutta method with adaptive time steps.
item.dc:creator: Sergey Matveev

item.title: Open Quantum Time Crystals without External Thermodynamic Resources: Go and No-Go Theorems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09540v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time crystals are phases of matter that spontaneously break time-translation symmetry. They have been ruled out in the ground and Gibbs states of isolated systems with only short-range interactions, yet they have been proposed and observed experimentally in nonequilibrium settings such as Floquet and open systems. However, existing proposals for time crystals in open quantum systems require an external supply of thermodynamic resources, such as work or energetic coherence. Whether coupling to an environment, without any such resource supply, can induce a time crystal absent in the isolated system remains open. Here, we answer this question systematically. We first construct an explicit model and prove that coupling to an environment can activate a time crystal absent in the isolated system, even without such resource supply. We consider Lindblad master equations with (i) time-independent Hamiltonian and jump operators, (ii) time-translation covariance, and (iii) detailed balance---conditions that hold in standard derivations unless thermodynamic resources are supplied externally. Our model satisfies these conditions, and the activation occurs in a stationary state of both the isolated and open systems. We give several implementations of this dynamics with a zero-temperature Gibbs environment, a time-independent, energy-conserving interaction, and only short-range Hamiltonians, one of which exactly reproduces the time-crystalline periodicity. We then prove a no-go theorem: under (i)--(iii), activation can arise only from an environment-induced Hamiltonian term, not from dissipation. Our results show that time crystals can be activated in open systems without external resource supply and identify the physical requirements on the system and environment for this activation through our general no-go theorem.
item.dc:creator: Yuri Ogami, Hiroyasu Tajima

item.title: Modular Hamiltonian and Typicality of Degenerate States
item.description: arXiv:2611.09595v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Free fermions exhibit Eigenstate Typicality (ET) meaning that the reduced density matrix, $\rho$, of a small spatial subsystem of a {\sl single}, typical, excited energy eigenstate is gaussian with a modular hamiltonian, $h \equiv -\log \rho$, asymptotically proportional to the free fermion hamiltonian. In effect, the ET may be thought of as providing an independent route to establishing the Fermi-Dirac (FD) distribution for free fermions. We revisit this argument for fermions belonging to a superposition of degenerate eigenstates. Specifically, we show that the modular hamiltonian corresponding to a superposition of degenerate eigenstates in a 1-d free fermion lattice system is interacting, and therefore the reduced density matrix for the subsystem is not gaussian. Measurements of the single particle distribution of a small subsystem would then exhibit non-thermal deviations from the FD distribution. These features may be traced to a violation of Wick's theorem for the chosen excited state. We develop a perturbation theory for the modular hamiltonian corresponding to a weak mixture of degenerate states and study the modular hamiltonian (exactly) computationally. Finally, we speculate that initial conditions in a realistic fermi system evolving towards equilibrium might be encoded in the interaction terms of the modular hamiltonian and consequent correlations of fermions.
item.dc:creator: Gregory C. Levine, Goncalo C. Oliveira

item.title: Arrival-time problem in the quantum information era - observation of a Zeno crossover in monitored arrival-time distributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09814v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When does a quantum particle arrive at a detector? The temporal distributions of itinerant quantum particles have been debated since the birth of quantum mechanics. Here we study the arrival-time problem in periodically monitored spin chains and quantum circuits. The arrival dynamics exhibits two regimes, the quantum Zeno and the low-monitoring regime, separated by an optimal monitoring period set by the single-particle bandwidth. In support of the theory, on superconducting quantum hardware, we measure arrival-time distributions for single and multiple interacting particles in one- and two-dimensional circuits. The measured distributions resolve both regimes and agree closely with quantum-trajectory theory. The crossover persists in interacting many-particle systems: the optimal monitoring point is preserved while many-body interference reshapes the distributions. Zeno suppression likewise persists in two-dimensional geometry. Together, these results show that the two regimes are a generic feature of monitored propagation rather than a single-particle effect. To our knowledge, our work constitutes the first experimental measurement of arrival-time distributions in a monitored quantum transport setting, addressing one of the longest-standing problems in quantum mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Yousef Mafi, K. G. S. H. Gunawardana, Kim P\"oyh\"onen, Teemu Ojanen

item.title: Gibbsian Entropy for General Wigner Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a definition of non-equilibrium Gibbsian entropy applicable to general quantum systems, computable from Wigner functions, for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states. We show that while the Wigner function is a quasi-probability distribution, fundamental results linking observables in repeated observations to the function, such as the law of large numbers, the central limit theorem and, crucially, the relation between the entropy and the cumulant generating function continue to apply. This ideas are the core of the large deviation theory, which allow to formulate a positive-definite definition of entropy based on our ignorance of the underlying state structure after repeated measurements of cumulants. This new definition is a parallel to the Gibbs entropy formulation, but it can also be used in out-of-equilibrium regimes. Some important properties of this entropy are discussed. In addition we derive some information theory quantities such as relative entropy, conditional entropy, mutual information and R\'enyi entropy. We then compare the results with Wehrl entropy for the 1D harmonic oscillator, for pure and mixed states. We conclude the the work discussing potential applications of this new formalism, ranging from quantum correlations beyond entanglement to thermalization in closed quantum systems.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Rabelo-Soares, Yevgeniy Kovchegov, Giorgio Torrieri

item.title: On deforming and breaking integrability
item.description: arXiv:2603.17018v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we study nearest-neighbour deformations of integrable models. After expanding in the deformation parameter, we identify four possible types of deformations. First there are deformations that simply break or preserve integrability. Then we find two different subtle cases. The first case is where the deformation is only integrable if all orders of the deformation parameter are taken into account. An example of these are the long-range deformations that appear in holographic models. The second case is when the deformation is perturbatively integrable to some order in the deformation parameter but can not be extended to an integrable model. In this paper we work this out for the XXZ spin chain and discuss the level statistics of each of these cases. We find numerical evidence that the onset of chaos occurs differently in each of these models. For the perturbatively integrable models, we find that the deformation strength at which chaos appears demonstrates a volume-scaling intermediate between strong and weak integrability breaking models.
item.dc:creator: Ysla F. Adans, Marius de Leeuw, Tristan McLoughlin

item.title: Universal Pareto fronts and trade-off relations in multi-objective optimization of thermal machines
item.description: arXiv:2603.19885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The performance of thermal machines is characterized with several, often competing quantities, such as power, efficiency, energy waste, and resilience to environmental noise. We employ multi-objective optimization to find the best thermal machines operating in the irreversible linear-response regime. We derive exact analytical parameterizations for the optimal (Pareto) fronts associated with mean extracted power, efficiency, entropy production and the amplitude of power fluctuations. These optimal fronts set the quantitative fundamental limits for the performance of linear-response machines, which are achieved under tight coupling conditions (endoreversible machines). The geometry of the fronts is universal: two-, three-, and four-objective trade-offs follow analytical formulae that do not depend on the value of any physical parameter of the machine. Furthermore, we test our results with existing experimental data from different physical systems operating also beyond the linear regime, ranging from atomic to macroscopic scales, and including single-atom engines, colloidal systems, macroscopic engines and power plants.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e A. Almanza-Marrero, \'Edgar Rold\'an, Gonzalo Manzano

item.title: Feedback percolation on complex networks
item.description: arXiv:2603.22089v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Traditional percolation theory assumes static microscopic rules, limiting its ability to describe real-world complex systems where macroscopic order actively regulates local interactions. Here, we introduce feedback percolation, an unified framework that dynamically couples the microscopic activation probability to the macroscopic size of the giant component. We show that this simple feedback mechanism produces a rich variety of behaviors both analytically and numerically. Depending on the feedback functions, the system exhibits explosive discontinuous jumps, hybrid transitions, limit-cycle oscillations, and routes to chaos, absent in classical percolation. Our findings establish that macroscopic feedback provides a unifying physical mechanism for phenomena ranging from self-regulating oscillations to systemic infrastructure collapse.
item.dc:creator: Hoseung Jang, Ginestra Bianconi, Byungjoon Min

item.title: Thermodynamic Approach to Momentum Transport in Dense Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2606.10858v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a new framework for extending Chapman-Enskog theory beyond the hard-sphere fluid model. Rather than relying on effective hard sphere diameters, the approach makes use of on an exchange function which can be related to the thermodynamic properties of the system. We show that two existing extensions, including modified Enskog theory (MET), fit into this new framework. Based on our approach, we propose an alternative to MET that takes into account the potential interaction energy associated with the inter-particle interactions in the fluid. The proposed expression is applied to predicting the shear viscosity of several different simulated fluid models across a wide set of densities $0.05 \leq \rho^* \leq 0.8$ and temperatures $1.5 \leq T^* \leq 4.0$ in Lennard-Jones units. The fluid models considered include both the Weeks-Chandler-Anderson (WCA) fluid and the Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid. At low and intermediate density, here taken to be $\rho^* \leq 0.3$, we report mean relative prediction errors between $2\%$ and $4\%$ for both these. Across all densities considered, the largest mean relative errors reported are $4.4\%$ and $8.1\%$ for the WCA fluid and LJ fluid respectively. We also investigate other interaction models, including a diatomic molecular model, in order to better understand the limitations of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Devik Fjeldstad, Jonas Bueie, Astrid S. de Wijn

item.title: Transport and thermalization under noncommuting localized constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.23781v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the effects of spatially localized conserved quantities on transport and thermalization in quantum and classical many-body systems. We consider several related models: the integrable quantum Volterra model, its nonintegrable classical limit, and two cellular automata derived from the latter. Although localized constraints are often associated with lattice gauge theories, our models do not admit such an interpretation. In systems with discrete degrees of freedom, these constraints induce uniform fragmentation of the Hilbert or configuration space. In the quantum Volterra model, we derive an exact mapping of the dynamics within each Hilbert-space fragment onto a quantum chiral Potts chain. We find that energy transport is ballistic, with identical transport coefficients across all fragments. In the nonintegrable classical limit, energy transport is diffusive, and we similarly find the diffusion constant to be independent of whether or not the constraints are fixed (resolved). Finally, in the cellular automata, we show that, despite leaving transport unaffected, localized constraints lead to a strong breakdown of local ergodicity.
item.dc:creator: Amir Nesturov, Attila Tak\'acs, Lenart Zadnik

item.title: Limit cycles in periodically driven open quantum systems
item.description: arXiv:1908.03900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the long-time behavior of quantum N-level systems that are coupled to a Markovian environment and subject to periodic driving. As our main result, we obtain a general algebraic condition ensuring that all solutions of a periodic quantum master equation with Lindblad form approach a unique limit cycle. Quite intuitively, this criterion requires that the dissipative terms of the master equation connect all subspaces of the system Hilbert space during an arbitrarily small fraction of the cycle time. Our results provide a natural extension of Spohn's algebraic condition for the approach to equilibrium to systems with external driving.
item.dc:creator: Paul Menczel, Kay Brandner

item.title: Concentration of ergotropy in quantum many-body systems
item.description: arXiv:2412.19801v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ergotropy$\unicode{x2014}$the maximal amount of unitarily extractable work$\unicode{x2014}$quantifies the "charge level" of a quantum battery. We prove that, in large many-body batteries, it exhibits a concentration of measure phenomenon. Namely, the ergotropy almost coincides with its average for almost all states sampled from the Hilbert$\unicode{x2013}$Schmidt measure. Importantly, the average ergotropy is macroscopic, scaling with the number of particles in the system. This occurs despite the von Neumann entropy also concentrating around a macroscopic average, a surprising coexistence since high entropy is commonly associated with effective thermality and thus passivity. We establish these results by proving that ergotropy, as a function of the state, is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the Bures distance and by applying L\'evy's measure concentration lemma. Furthermore, we numerically extend our findings to the Bures measure, which represents the situation with the least amount of prior information about the state. Our continuity and concentration bounds open a new perspective on the noise-robustness of quantum many-body batteries and lay the groundwork for further rigorous studies of their charge stability and work extraction with limited prior knowledge.
item.dc:creator: Karen Hovhannisyan, Rick P. A. Simon, Janet Anders

item.title: Imprints of information scrambling on eigenstates of a quantum chaotic system
item.description: arXiv:2507.02853v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How are the spatial and temporal patterns of information scrambling in locally interacting quantum many-body systems imprinted on the eigenstates of the system's time-evolution operator? We address this question by identifying statistical correlations among sets of minimally four eigenstates that provide a unified framework for various measures of information scrambling. These include operator mutual information and operator entanglement entropy of the time-evolution operator, as well as more conventional diagnostics such as two-point dynamical correlations and out-of-time-ordered correlators. We demonstrate this framework by deriving exact results for eigenstate correlations in a minimal model of quantum chaos -- Floquet dual-unitary circuits. These results reveal not only the butterfly effect and the information lightcone, but also finer structures of scrambling within the lightcone. Our work thus shows how the eigenstates of a chaotic system can encode the full spatiotemporal anatomy of quantum chaos, going beyond the descriptions offered by random matrix theory and the eigenstate thermalisation hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Bikram Pain, Ratul Thakur, Sthitadhi Roy

item.title: A Machine Learning study of the two-dimensional antiferromagnetic $Q$-state Potts model on the square lattice
item.description: arXiv:2512.06762v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The critical phenomena of 2D antiferromagnetic $Q$-state Potts model on the square lattice with $Q=2,3,4,5$ and 6 are investigated using supervised neural networks (NN). Conventional supervised and unsupervised NNs either fail or have difficulty in identifying the correct critical behaviors of these models. Remarkably, despite the fact that the NNs employed here are trained with a particular fixed type training set which contains no information about the considered models (except for $Q=2$), they correctly compute the critical temperatures for the studied physical systems. Particularly, the NN outcomes suggest convincingly that the $Q=3$ model is critical only at zero temperature and $Q=4,5,6$ models remain disordered at all temperatures. Apart from the studied models, our NNs trained with exactly the same training set have successfully determined the critical temperature(s) and the nature of the associated phase transition(s) of another physical system differing dramatically from those considered here. Therefore, our NN has the potential to be a universally applicable NN model in studying phase transitions.
item.dc:creator: Shang-Wei Li, Kai-Wei Huang, Chien-Ting Chen, Fu-Jiun Jiang

item.title: Embedding stochastic dynamics in latent manifolds of recurrent neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2602.14885v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a theoretical framework for understanding computation in biological neural circuits through their ability to support rich time-dependent behaviour. Whilst high-dimensional by construction, they can be used to encode low-dimensional dynamical systems, for example by restricting to low-rank connectivity, hence mirroring the emergence of latent neural manifolds found in empirical neural data. Here, we exploit a relationship between RNNs and a class of universal approximators to train networks that can represent arbitrary, nonlinear stochastic differential equations (SDEs), with given drift and diffusion coefficients, within a low-dimensional latent subspace. We show that RNNs can faithfully embed the drift and diffusion of a given SDE, including nonlinear and nonequilibrium dynamics such as chaotic attractors. We apply this approach by constructing RNN realisations of stochastic systems that transiently explore various attractors through both input-driven switching and autonomous transitions driven by nonequilibrium currents, which we interpret as models of associative and sequential (episodic) memory. To elucidate how these dynamics are encoded in the network, we introduce decompositions of the RNN based on its asymmetric connectivity and its time-irreversibility. Our results show that neural populations can implement a broad class of stochastic dynamics within low-dimensional manifolds, unifying ideas from the dynamics of neural computation, the theory of neural manifolds, associative memory, and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Ram\'on Nartallo-Kaluarachchi, Renaud Lambiotte, Alain Goriely

item.title: Distinct mechanisms underlying in-context learning in transformers
item.description: arXiv:2604.12151v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern distributed networks, notably transformers, acquire a remarkable ability (termed `in-context learning') to adapt their computation to input statistics, such that a fixed network can be applied to data from a broad range of systems. Here, we provide a complete mechanistic characterization of this behavior in transformers trained on a finite set $S$ of discrete Markov chains. The transformer displays four algorithmic phases, characterized by whether the network memorizes and generalizes, and whether it uses 1-point or 2-point statistics. We show that the four phases are implemented by multi-layer subcircuits that exemplify two qualitatively distinct mechanisms for implementing context-adaptive computations. Minimal models isolate the key features of both motifs. Memorization and generalization phases are delineated by two boundaries that depend on data diversity, $K = |S|$. The first ($K_1^\ast$) is set by a kinetic competition between subcircuits and the second ($K_2^\ast$) is set by a representational bottleneck. A symmetry-constrained theory of a transformer's training dynamics explains the sharp transition from 1-point to 2-point generalization and identifies key features of the loss landscape that allow the network to generalize. Put together, we show that transformers develop distinct subcircuits to implement in-context learning and identify conditions that favor certain mechanisms over others.
item.dc:creator: Cole Gibson, Wenping Cui, Gautam Reddy

item.title: Electron Coherence and Dephasing by Quasi-Static Coulomb Fluctuations in Classical Ionic Media
item.description: arXiv:2605.18187v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a microscopic theory of quantum-particle propagation through quasi-static electrostatic fluctuations of a classical one-component plasma. The RPA potential is Gaussian but has an unscreened $1/r$ correlation tail, which makes the disorder-averaged retarded Green function infrared sensitive. Its eikonal attenuation scale is $\ell_{\rm w}=k^2/G$ for $g=G/k^3\ll1$, with the formal strong-saddle asymptote $\ell_{\rm s}=(4\sqrt[3]{2}/3)G^{-1/3}$ for $g\gg1$. For a slab of thickness $d$, the retarded--advanced mutual-coherence kernel is infrared finite: the coherence decays algebraically for $\lambda_D\ll\rho\ll d$ and saturates at larger transverse separation. Thus equilibrium ionic-density fluctuations constitute a distinct quasi-static dephasing channel with a nonexponential coherence law. A finite coherence radius exists only when the saturation threshold is crossed. Relativistic paraxial reduction gives $a_{\rm rel}=1/(\hbar v)$ and the finite high-energy limit $1/(\hbar c)$. The ionic contribution is very small at conventional TEM energies for a $100\,\mathrm{nm}$ water-like layer. Within the quasi-static model it grows for thicker samples and lower-energy electrons, while sub-keV transmission through liquid water is strongly limited by inelastic scattering.
item.dc:creator: Yury A. Budkov

item.title: Broadband molecular dynamics simulation of confined Brownian motion
item.description: arXiv:2606.24291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Molecular dynamics with an explicit solvent resolves the hydrodynamic response of a Brownian colloid in bulk and near a rigid wall over acoustic, inertial, and diffusive time scales. Bulk spectra establish a continuum reference and reveal departures associated with discrete-solvent dynamics. Under confinement, thermal spectra provide a measurement of the space-dependent added mass, while velocity autocorrelations determine space-dependent, anisotropic hydrodynamic memory and diffusion. All together, these measurements connect the enhanced added mass and reduced mobility near a wall, and probe the discrete-continuum crossover.
item.dc:creator: Quentin Thomas, Clara Mefo Sop, Maxime Lavaud, Yacine Amarouchene, Thomas Salez, Pascal Damman

item.title: Controlling Waiting Time Statistics in Monitored Collective Spins: Mitigating Detector's Resolution Barrier in Measurement-Induced Phase Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2607.01332v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In collective dissipative spin systems, the postselection barrier can be partially mitigated; however, a further obstacle may be posed by the finite temporal resolution of detectors. In this work, we investigate how initial-state inhomogeneities can control waiting-time statistics between quantum jumps, thereby mitigating the detector-resolution problem. We consider a collectively monitored spin model with a boundary time-crystalline phase, introducing inhomogeneity by partitioning the ensemble into two subsystems rotated by an angle $\theta$. We find that the measurement-induced phase transition survives under inhomogeneities, with different entanglement scaling regimes. The waiting time increases with $\theta$, scaling as $1/N$ but with a prefactor strongly enhanced by orders of magnitude, and in the anti-aligned limit $\theta = \pi$ it remains finite, fully resolving the resolution barrier. This mitigation, however, comes at a cost: the entanglement saturation time becomes significantly longer, partially reintroducing the postselection barrier. Our results highlight a trade-off between detector resolution and postselection overhead, with direct implications for the experimental observation of measurement-induced phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Tanbir Islam, Fernando Iemini

item.title: A Kernel-Based Density of States Estimator for Quantum Computing
item.description: arXiv:2607.24972v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a quantum kernel method for estimating the density of states (DoS) of quantum many-body systems. The method exploits the Rodeo algorithm as a physical implementation, requiring no modification of its standard single-ancilla circuit. Averaging the Rodeo response over Haar-random input states reconstructs the DoS convolved with a spectral kernel whose analytical form is determined entirely by the probability distribution of the sampled evolution times. This establishes a direct quantum analogue of the classical Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM): Haar-random states perform stochastic trace estimation, while the temporal sampling distribution plays the role of the reconstruction kernel. We derive the estimator, quantify its statistical and systematic uncertainties, and establish an explicit correspondence between quantum reconstruction kernels and classical signal-processing window functions, enabling concepts such as spectral leakage, side-lobe attenuation, and main-lobe width to guide kernel design. The method is validated numerically on the one-dimensional transverse-field spin--$\sfrac{1}{2}$ and spin--$1$ Ising models, where the reconstructed density of states and the resulting thermodynamic observables agree with exact diagonalization within the estimated statistical uncertainties.
item.dc:creator: Julio Cesar Siqueira Rocha
